name: Proof by contrapositive
quick: Prove not Q implies not P to establish P implies Q.
definition: Keep the original domain. Assume the negation of the conclusion, deduce the negation of the hypothesis, then invoke logical equivalence.
example: To show an even square has an even integer root, show an odd integer has an odd square.
confusion: Reversing the implication without negating both sides gives the converse.

name: Does not divide
quick: $d\nmid n$ means there is no integer k with n=dk.
definition: The slashed divisibility bar negates an integer divisibility proposition. It is not a fraction or an inequality.
example: $4\nmid6$, because no integer multiplied by 4 gives 6.
confusion: A nonzero remainder rules out divisibility; a real quotient always existing does not establish it.

name: Prime number
section: An even product has an even factor
quick: An integer greater than 1 with only positive divisors 1 and itself.
definition: A prime cannot be factored into two positive integers both greater than 1. The domain restriction excludes 1, zero, and negative integers.
confusion: Divisibility properties demonstrated for 2 do not automatically hold for every positive divisor.

name: Quotient and remainder
quick: Write n as a whole multiple of a positive divisor plus a bounded leftover.
definition: For positive integer d and any integer n, division with remainder writes $n=dk+r$ with integer quotient k and $0\leq r<d$.
example: $-1=3(-1)+2$ has quotient -1 and remainder 2 on division by 3.
confusion: The remainder convention is nonnegative even when the quotient is negative.

name: Irrational number
quick: A real number that cannot be an integer fraction with nonzero denominator.
definition: Irrationality is the negation of rationality within the real numbers. Rationality often gives a useful representation for a contrapositive proof.
example: If $x=a/b$ is rational, $x^2=a^2/b^2$ is rational; therefore irrational $x^2$ forces irrational x.
confusion: An irrational input can have a rational square.

name: Proof by contradiction
quick: Assume the whole claim is false and derive incompatible facts.
definition: For a claim S, assume its negation temporarily. A valid impossibility then rules out that assumption in classical logic. For an implication, assume both its hypothesis and its failed conclusion.
example: To prove there is no greatest integer, assume M is greatest; the integer M+1 contradicts that property.
confusion: Contraposition need only assume not Q; contradiction of P implies Q assumes P as well.
